answer.html: Do work to pull them farther apart. Opposite charges attract, so you must pull against the force; the work you do is stored as electric potential energy.

Potential difference is work per unit charge: 𝛥𝑉= 𝑊/ 𝑞′, so 𝑊= 𝑞′𝛥𝑉.
For the 4.0 𝜇C charge, 𝑊= (4.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>)(12) = 4.8 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> J, but 𝛥𝑉= 𝑊/ 𝑞′ is still 12 V.

answer.html: 𝑊= 2.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> J. The work is proportional to the test charge (doubling the charge doubles the work), while the potential difference stays 12 V because it does not depend on the test charge.

items.title: 53 (Example Problem 5 Practice 1): An oil drop between charged plates is rising at constant velocity. What forces act on it, and how do they compare?

answer.html: Three forces act on the drop (buoyancy is negligible): the downward weight 𝑚𝑔, a downward air-resistance (drag) force because the drop is moving up through the air, and the upward electric force 𝑞𝐸. At constant velocity the net force is zero, so 𝑞𝐸= 𝑚𝑔+ 𝐹<sub>drag</sub>; the electric force is larger than the weight alone.

items.title: Lesson 4 "Get It?" (lightning rod): Airplanes have thin, pointed "static wicks" on the trailing edges of their wings and tail. How do they help keep the plane's charge from building up?

answer.html: Charge on a conductor is most concentrated at sharp points, where it makes a very strong electric field. The strong field at a wick's tip ionizes the air there, so charge leaks off into the air gradually and quietly instead of building up on the plane and discharging suddenly.

items.title: 63 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 4): Explain to a friend how electric potential difference is related to work done on a charge, using an analogy to a hill.

answer.html: Electric potential energy is the energy a charge has because of where it is in an electric field, like a rock's energy because of its height on a hill. The potential difference is the energy change per unit charge, 𝛥𝑉= 𝑊/ 𝑞′, like the height difference between the bottom and top of the hill: it depends only on the two locations, and multiplying it by any charge gives the work needed to move that charge between them.

items.title: 69 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 4): A small conducting sphere of radius 2.0 cm carries −6.0 𝜇C. It touches a large neutral conducting sphere of radius 6.0 cm. What can be said about (a) their potentials, (b) their charges, and (c) the charge on each after they touch (capacitance of a sphere is proportional to its radius)?

body.html: Charge flows between touching conductors until there is no potential difference. Work (a): Touching makes one conductor, so the potential must be equal everywhere. Work (b): Total charge is conserved (−6.0 𝜇C) and it divides in proportion to capacitance (size), so the larger sphere holds the greater share. Work (c): The radii are in the ratio 2.0: 6.0 = 1: 3, so the charge is shared 1: 3.

answer.html: The two spheres are at the same potential. Answer (b): Their charges are not equal: the larger sphere holds more, and both are negative. Answer (c): The small sphere ends with −1.5 𝜇C and the large sphere with −4.5 𝜇C.

items.title: 70 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 4, Critical Thinking; Figure 32): A charged metal ball on an insulating handle is lowered into a hollow metal can and touches the inner wall. Why does all of its charge move onto the can, and why can the process be repeated again and again to build up more and more charge on the can?

body.html: Charge on a conductor sits on its outer surface, and the field inside a closed conductor is zero.

When the ball touches the inside wall they form one conductor, and the charge moves to the outer surface of the can at once. Inside the can the field of the can's charge is zero, so the ball feels no repulsion from the charge already on the can, however much is there. The ball is left neutral. Withdraw it, charge it again, and repeat.

answer.html: Inside the closed metal can the field of the can's charge is zero, so nothing repels more charge off the ball. The charge moves to the can's outer surface, and each repetition adds more net charge to the can.

items.title: Wrap-Up "Revisit the Phenomenon" and "CER: Explain Your Reasoning": Why does a rubbed balloon stick to a neutral wall? Does your evidence support your claim?

answer.html: Yes, the claim (the balloon's electric field polarizes the wall so the nearer, oppositely charged surface attracts the balloon more than the farther like charge repels it) is supported by the module: (1) charged objects attract neutral ones by charge separation (Lessons 1 and 2); (2) the force is stronger at shorter distances (Coulomb's law); (3) the balloon's field acts on the charges inside the wall; (4) the effect does not depend on the sign of the balloon's charge, and it fades as the charge leaks into the air. No revision is needed.

items.title: Wrap-Up "Data Analysis Lab" 2 (Evidence and Reasoning): Explain how you decided your rankings in the table above.

answer.html: The force on a charge in a field is 𝐹= 𝑞𝐸, so each force is the product of the charge and the field. B (3 × 150) and D (9 × 50) give the same product, 450, so they tie for the largest. Note that D has the largest charge and C has the largest field, but neither is the strongest force; the product decides the ranking.

items.title: Wrap-Up "STEM Unit Project" and "3D Thinking: Scientific Breakthroughs" (activities): (1) Summarize how the ideas of this module apply to an electrostatic air purifier that you design. (2) Describe a model of Earth's magnetosphere shielding the planet from the solar wind.

question.html: Physics idea / method: These are design or model-building tasks, not calculations. For the design project: summarize evidence from this module (charge conservation, Coulomb's law, fields, potential difference, energy stored in capacitors) and tie it to your device. For example, the purifier gives dust particles a charge, then passes them between oppositely charged plates where the field 𝐸= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑑 exerts a force 𝐹= 𝑞𝐸 that pulls them onto the plates. For the magnetosphere model: draw the Sun on one side with the solar wind streaming toward Earth, Earth with its magnetic field bubble (the magnetosphere) around it, a bow shock where the wind is slowed on the sunward side, and a long tail on the far side; label where charged particles are deflected.

answer.html: These are open-ended projects. A suggested outline is given above; no single numerical answer exists.

items.title: Lesson 4 "Explain" (Figure 23) Question: Explain how work and electric potential are related for the test charge.

answer.html: The electric potential difference is the work done moving the test charge divided by its charge, 𝛥𝑉= 𝑊/ 𝑞′. Positive work on a positive test charge raises its potential energy and gives a positive potential difference; the potential difference does not depend on the size of the test charge.

answer.html: 1 V/m = 1 N/C.

items.title: 66 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 4) Question: In a Millikan apparatus, the drop's net charge changes and it starts to fall. How should the

body.html: It falls when 𝑞𝐸< 𝑚𝑔, so its charge decreased in magnitude (or its mass increased). Balance needs 𝑞𝐸= 𝑚𝑔 again.
𝐸= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑑, so 𝑞𝛥𝑉/ 𝑑= 𝑚𝑔; if 𝑞 gets smaller, 𝛥𝑉 must get bigger: 𝛥𝑉<sup>new</sup> = 𝛥𝑉<sup>old</sup>(𝑞<sub>old</sub> / 𝑞<sub>new</sub>).

answer.html: Increase the potential difference between the plates (in proportion to the drop in charge) until the drop is held again.

items.title: 67 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 4) Question: If changing the potential difference has no effect on the falling drop, what does that say about

answer.html: The drop has become neutral (net charge zero), so the electric field exerts no force on it, whatever the voltage.

items.title: 69 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 4) Question: A small negatively charged conducting sphere touches a large positively charged conducting

question.html: sphere. What can be said about (a) their potentials, (b) their charges?

body.html: Charge flows between touching conductors until there is no potential difference. Work (a): Touching makes one conductor, so the potential must be equal everywhere. Work (b): Total charge is conserved. The charge divides in proportion to the capacitance (size) of the spheres, so the larger sphere ends up with the greater share. Part of the positive charge is cancelled by the negative charge, and the leftover has the sign of the larger original charge (here the large positive sphere is assumed to have the larger magnitude).

answer.html: The two spheres are at the same potential. Answer (b): Their charges are not equal: total charge is conserved and shared in proportion to size, with the larger sphere holding more. Both have the sign of the net total (positive if the large sphere's original charge outweighed the small sphere's).

items.title: 70 (Check Your Progress, Lesson 4, Critical Thinking; Figure 32) Question: Why does charge keep building up on the dome of a Van de Graaff generator, and why isn't it

question.html: repelled back onto the belt at B?

body.html: Charge on a conductor sits on its outer surface, and the field inside a closed conductor is zero.

At B the belt carries positive charge into the inside of the hollow dome and touches a brush or contact. Charge transfers to the dome (a conductor) and moves to its outer surface at once. Inside the dome the field is zero, so the charge on the dome exerts no repelling force on the belt at B, while the charges on the outside repel each other but are held by the dome's surface. The belt returns uncharged, and the process repeats.

answer.html: Inside the closed metal dome the field of the dome's charge is zero, so nothing repels charge off the belt at B; the charge moves onto the outer surface of the dome, leaving the dome with more and more net charge.

items.title: Wrap-Up "Revisit the Phenomenon" and "CER: Explain Your Reasoning" Question: Why does the rod cause the water to bend? Does your evidence support your claim?

answer.html: Yes, the claim (the rod's electric field polarizes the water so the nearer, oppositely charged side is attracted more than the far side is repelled) is supported by the module: (1) charged objects attract neutral ones by charge separation (Lessons 1 and 2); (2) force strength increases as distance decreases (Coulomb's law); (3) the field of the rod acts on the water's polar molecules; (4) the effect does not depend on the sign of the rod's charge. No revision is needed.

items.title: Wrap-Up "Data Analysis Lab" 2 (Evidence and Reasoning) Question: Explain how you decided your rankings.

answer.html: The force on a charge in a field is 𝐹= 𝑞𝐸, so each force is the product of the charge and the field. B has by far the largest field (600 N/C) and a large charge, so its force is the largest. A ( 3 × 70) and D (6 × 35) give the same product, 210, so they tie. E (8 × 10 = 80) is next, and C ( 3 × 20 = 60) is smallest. Note that a greater charge or a greater field alone does not decide the ranking; the product does.

items.title: Wrap-Up "STEM Unit Project" and "3D Thinking: Scientific Breakthroughs" (activities)

question.html: Physics idea / method: These are design or model-building tasks, not calculations. For the STEM project: summarize evidence from this module (charge conservation, Coulomb's law, fields, potential difference, energy stored in capacitors) and tie it to your energy conversion device. For the Local Interstellar Cloud model: draw the Sun at the center, the heliosphere (the Sun's magnetic bubble) around it, the Local Interstellar Cloud outside with the cloud's magnetic field pressing in on the heliosphere, and label the hot gas bubble outside the cloud.

answer.html: These are open-ended projects. A suggested outline is given above; no single numerical answer exists.
